description.x: This session aims at developing an understanding amongst the students on the environmental crisis, generation of waste poses in the modern day. This session takes a historical perspective on kinds of waste and how it has changed over the years.

sequence.x: Pictionary - Students will be called out at random in front of the class, and will be asked to draw anything that comes to their mind when they hear the word “waste”. The student will be given 20-30 seconds to draw on the board, and the class will guess simultaneously. The first one to guess correctly will be the one to come and draw next. We shall have 8-10 such rounds.

The game will help us recognize what student’s think of waste, as they might draw things associated with waste which can range from a banana peel to a waste picker. It’ll act as a fun start to the class and help us carry the topic forward.

Our quest of understanding waste and its management will begin with, firstly, asking the students what they think waste is and its source, and improper waste management and its impact on the ecosystem in order to facilitate brainstorming and engagement from the very start, with a special focus on plastic waste pollution.
After asking students and jotting down their knowledge of waste, proper definitions will be provided of waste, its sources, types, impact and information on the global waste production scenario.

To establish why waste and its management are being discussed, a film will be shown that shows the impact of improper waste management. “How plastic is so much worse than you think!” (How plastic harms the environment in different ways and how to reduce our plastic footprint) https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=n4SmwBFbhEM

discussion.x: The statistics relating to production, re-use and dumping of waste to be drawn on charts/PPT and put up prior to discussion and may be referred to during discussions.
What is waste, types, sources and quantity
What is Waste - Waste (or wastes) is unwanted or unusable materials. A substance becomes waste because it is either discarded after primary use, or is worthless, defective and of no use.
Sources – Municipal (household, commercial, construction, institutions, treatment plants), agricultural and Industrial
Types - Solid waste like plastic, food, construction waste, waste water like sewage; chemical waste like radioactive waste, e-waste, batteries, pesticides, herbicides, and bio-medical waste.
10% of the total human waste comprises plastic. Facilitators may ask students where they use plastic in their daily lives.

Plastic came to be commonly used from the 1950s onwards. In the last 69 years, we have produced about 9.2 billion tons of plastic (which is equivalent to 1 billion elephants, 10,000 blue whales or 15 jumbo jets, can bury Manhattan under more than two miles of trash. Facilitator can ask students to come up with more size equivalents and also ask them to consider that one 2 litre coke bottle weighs only 42 grams)
Disposal of waste
Ask students to think of answers for the following questions:
what they think happens to the waste generated from each of these sources.
What will happen if they throw a banana peel, a piece of paper, an aluminum foil, and an empty chips packet on the soil.
What do they see when they spill one drop, then one mug then one bucket of each of ink, oil, muddy water, and milk into one bucket of water.
With the above, concepts of ‘carrying capacity’ and ‘self-recovery’ of the planet may be introduced.
What will happen if they throw each of the above, in a closed container, first separately, then together.
With the above, concept of proper disposal of waste may be introduced. What do they think is the best method to dispose of food waste, metal, and then plastic.
what happens with the waste collected from home- whether they are familiar with the role of rag pickers.
What is segregation – why is it important
Have they seen a landfill- do they think waste is segregated in a landfill o Methods of waste disposal- recycling, incineration, landfill
Consequences of waste
Impact- One truckload of garbage is dumped in the ocean, every minute.
On land- landfill, aesthetic concerns, polluted soil with toxics.

Water-unsanitary landfills- seep into groundwater, solid waste dumped on waterbodies accumulates and forms a layer which can burn (Bellundur lake in Bangalore example), open defecation problems, reduction of dissolved oxygen and concept of ‘dying of waterbodies’
Air- Odour, Noxious gases, Methane production, spontaneous fires- burns all kinds of waste which releases further toxic gases (e.g. if plastic or hazardous wastes are burnt)
Humans – People living in unhygienic conditions are already vulnerable- health and mortality
Economy – cost, poverty
Wildlife – health and mortality
Impact of plastic pollution in the oceans- impact on aquatic life, food chain.
Plastic Waste in World/Basic Plastic Pollution Facts

By the end of this century (2100), garbage will be collected at the rate of 11 million tons per day globally, more than three times today’s rate. It implies that the garbage-generation which amounted to 3.5 million tons per day in 2010 will become 6 million tons per day by 2025. At present, people of India produce about 62 million tons of solid-waste annually. Out of this, 45 million tons of garbage are left untreated and disposed of by civic agencies in an unscientific manner.
Also, 50% of this plastic has only been used once or as commonly called is ‘single-use plastic’.
Out of the total plastic produced, 75% is waste (6.9 Billion tons).
And of that waste, we have recycled only 0.6 billion tons and have no way of disposing the remaining 6.3 billion tons.
Impact of Plastic Pollution
About 8.8 million tons of plastic is dumped in the oceans by us, annually.

Nearly 700 species, including endangered ones, are known to have been affected by it. 100,000 marine creatures a year die from plastic entanglement and these are the ones found. By 2050, virtually every seabird species on the planet will be eating plastic.
Scientists have found microplastics in 114 aquatic species, from zoo-plankton to whales, and more than half of those end up on our dinner plates.
Plastic Waste in India

India produces 25,940 tonnes of plastic waste every day, out of which 60% is recycled, thus the remaining pollutes water bodies and land (CPCB, 2015). Most common sources of plastic waste are films, wrapping materials, shopping and garbage bags, fluid containers, clothing, toys, household and industrial products and building materials. Of which, packaging is the single largest application of plastics, accounting for 43% of all plastics; followed by infrastructure (21%), automotive industry (16%), agriculture (2%) and others (18%) [FICCI].

A survey of 60 Indian cities by the CPCB in 2015 found that plastic accounts for 8% of all solid waste, with the figure going up to over 10% in nine cities, including Delhi that produces the maximum plastic waste in the country, followed by Chennai and Kolkata.
Plastic Waste Management Waste management begins at source reduction where Refuse, Reduce and Reuse are focussed upon. They are preferred over recycling as they use no energy.

The plastic waste then collected is either recycled, incinerated, dumped in landfills or water bodies, or sometimes used in pyrolysis (a waste-to-energy method), co-processing with cement and polymer-bitumen roads.
Recycling
8-10% of the total waste produced is plastic of which approximately [47%] is recycled, much greater than the global average of around 20%.
Problem of non-segregation

Role of rag pickers. Waste pickers, in India, are the backbone of waste collection and recycling sector. Yet they constitute 0.1% of the urban work force (2013). They collect and recycle 20-25% of total waste, in cities like Delhi, every day.

India recycled 47% of total plastic waste in contrast to China(11%), the USA (3.5%), South Africa (15%), and UK (7%). There are nearly 20 thousand industries in India in plastics recycling process with total daily capacity of 1 KT. Although plastic recycling in India is mostly mechanized, but generally operates at a low level of organization. There were over 2000 recycling units in India along with 2,500 pelletizers. Easy availability of low-cost manpower and exclusive market for the lower-quality products have helped in ﬂourishing those recycle industries in India.
Incineration

Incineration changes the form of the waste, reduces its volume and weight, but does not destroy many of its hazardous components. Incineration techniques causes air pollution and causes release of toxic gases like carbon monoxide, chlorine, hydrochloric acid, dioxin, furans, amines, nitrides, styrene, benzene, 1, 3- butadiene, tera-chloro methane and acetaldehyde. In fact, two new forms of waste are produced: gaseous emission and solid residue. In Delhi, 12% of the waste produced is incinerated (2015). India has 5 operational Waste-to-Energy plants which have a capacity of 66.5 MW.

In fact, two new forms of waste are produced: gaseous emission and solid residue. Gases exit from smokestacks of the incinerators and solid residue include ash from combustion chamber (bottom ash) and fly ash that rises up the smokestacks.
Landfills and Water Bodies
India discards around 0.6 million tons of plastic in the ocean, annually.
